name: Ampicillin
route_note: Mainly IV/IM in hospital; oral use largely replaced by amoxicillin. Also combined with sulbactam (Unasyn).

discovery.note: Made by acylating 6-aminopenicillanic acid with a D-phenylglycine side chain. Year of discovery (1958), per Wikipedia.

tagline: The first broad-spectrum penicillin, still key for neonatal sepsis and listeria
summary: Ampicillin, launched by Beecham in 1961, was the first penicillin active against a range of Gram-negative bacteria. It remains an important injectable agent, notably with gentamicin for neonatal sepsis and for Listeria and enterococcal infections.
mechanism: Ampicillin binds penicillin-binding proteins and inhibits the final transpeptidation step of peptidoglycan synthesis, leading to cell lysis.

The amino group in its side chain improves passage through Gram-negative outer-membrane porins, but the drug is hydrolysed by common plasmid beta-lactamases such as TEM-1, which spread rapidly among Enterobacterales and Haemophilus from the 1960s–70s.
uses: Neonatal sepsis and meningitis (with an aminoglycoside or cefotaxime)
Enterococcal infections including endocarditis (with gentamicin or ceftriaxone)
Susceptible respiratory, urinary and gastrointestinal infections

history.title: 6-APA
history.detail: Beecham isolates 6-aminopenicillanic acid, enabling semi-synthetic penicillins.

history.title: Launch
history.detail: Ampicillin is introduced as Penbritin, the first broad-spectrum penicillin.

history.title: TEM-1 beta-lactamase
history.detail: The plasmid-mediated TEM-1 beta-lactamase is described in an E. coli isolate from Greece, foreshadowing widespread ampicillin resistance.

history.title: Amoxicillin
history.detail: Beecham launches amoxicillin, which largely replaces oral ampicillin.

facts: The TEM beta-lactamase is named after Temoniera, the Greek patient from whom the first resistant isolate was obtained.
